header.title: Traditional AGV Dispatching in an Automated Container Terminal under Stochastic Conditions

rows: Briskorn inventory rule, nearest vehicle first come first served (NV/FCFS), fixed groups
Memetic search on the expected times, plan made once then followed
Rolling horizon, re-plans as the terminal evolves
Preference learning or imitation of the benchmark
Best achievable, as it knows all future times

findings.text: The simulator reproduces hand-worked cases to within a millionth of a second, and its rack rules give the hand-worked answer in every check.
findings.conditions: 5 hand-built cases · 96 random runs · 756 automatic tests

findings.text: Four AGVs per crane is the operating fleet. The best rule then keeps each crane waiting 5.7 s per container, against 13.3 s for random dispatching, so the choice of dispatcher clearly matters.

stages.question: Can the simulator be trusted?
stages.why: Every later number depends on the simulator moving AGVs exactly as the layout and vehicle data say.

stages.question: Where do dispatching decisions matter?
stages.why: Before adding randomness, the fleet size and rule settings must be chosen where the choice of dispatcher can make a difference.

stages.question: Is the optimiser strong enough to serve as a benchmark?
stages.why: The benchmark and the optimised plans both come from a search, so the search itself has to be checked first.

stages.question: What happens when crane times become random?
stages.why: This is the core test of the traditional baselines, and the reason a real-time dispatcher is needed.

notation: How much crane cycle times vary. Each cycle is drawn as $c_i \sim U\big((1-\delta)\,\bar c,\ (1+\delta)\,\bar c\big)$ with $\bar c = 75$ s, so with $\delta = 0.4$ each cycle takes between 45 and 105 s instead of exactly 75 s.

The number after ± is half the width of a 95% confidence interval over the $n$ seeds, $\bar I \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\, s/\sqrt{n}$, where $s$ is the standard deviation over the seeds and $t = 2.045$ for 30 seeds.

Each seed fixes one instance and one draw of crane times, and every method runs on the same seeds. The gap between two methods A and B is therefore measured seed by seed, $\Delta = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}(I_{A,k}-I_{B,k})$, under identical conditions (common random numbers).
Nearest vehicle, first come first served. A free AGV takes the oldest released job.
The benchmark sees all realised crane times in advance. No real dispatcher can, so it shows how much room is left.

cards.title: The simulator reproduces hand-worked cases exactly
cards.lead: Yes. In five hand-built cases with 190 event times and 308 path segments, the largest gap is 5 × 10⁻⁷ s, below the required millionth of a second. The rack rules give the hand-worked answer in every check, and in 96 random runs on the full yard no two AGVs ever used one rack at the same time.
cards.body: The five cases were built on the earlier 5-block section of the yard, where every path can be traced on paper. The rack rules of the current yard are checked on separate small cases. A suite of 756 automatic tests repeats all of these checks after every change to the code.
details: Single trips, rack visits, lane booking at the buffer, a crane with all four lanes full, a single open lane, parking, and loads fetched from racks.
AGVs drive at 6 m/s on straights and 3 m/s in turns, with 0.5 m/s² acceleration and braking (Luo, 2016).
Driving 15.5 m into the rack lane and back at 1 m/s, as in the earlier 46 s visit. Raising and lowering the platform take 10 s each, an assumption since no published value was found.
Every event time must agree within 10⁻⁶ s, every segment length within 10⁻⁶ m.
cards.label: Experiment 1.1 · Simulator check

design.question: Does the simulator move AGVs, cranes and racks exactly as the layout, the vehicle data and the rules say?
design.why: Every later number comes from the simulator. If it moved AGVs wrongly, every comparison of dispatchers would be wrong with it.
design.vary: Small cases that each exercise one rule. Single trips, lane booking under the crane, waiting at a full crane, parking, choosing the nearest free rack, a block whose racks are all busy, and the steps of a rack visit.
design.fixed: Each case is worked out by hand before the simulator is run, without using any of its code.
design.measure: The largest gap between the simulator and the hand-worked value, over every event time and every path segment.
design.decide: The simulator passes only if every gap is below a millionth of a second and every rack rule gives the hand-worked answer.

maths.step: Speed where two path segments meet
maths.text: A path is a chain of straights (at most $v = 6$ m/s) and turns (at most 3 m/s, *Luo, 2016*). The AGV starts and stops at rest and accelerates and brakes at $a = 0.5$ m/s². Going forward, the speed $w_{i+1}$ at the end of segment $i$ of length $L_i$ is what the AGV can reach from $w_i$. A backward pass then lowers it wherever the AGV could not brake in time.

Inside a segment the AGV speeds up, cruises and slows down. If the peak speed $v_p$ stays below the limit $V$ there is no cruise. For a 100 m straight from rest to rest, $v_p = \sqrt{50} = 7.07$ m/s is above 6 m/s, so the AGV cruises.
maths.tex: $$v_p = \sqrt{a L + \tfrac{1}{2}(v_0^{2}+v_1^{2})},\qquad t = \begin{cases}\dfrac{2v_p - v_0 - v_1}{a} & v_p \le V\\[8pt] \dfrac{2V - v_0 - v_1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{V}\Big(L - \dfrac{V^{2}-v_0^{2}}{2a} - \dfrac{V^{2}-v_1^{2}}{2a}\Big) & v_p > V\end{cases}$$

maths.text: The AGV drives $\ell = 15.5$ m into the rack lane and back at $v_r = 1$ m/s, and raises and lowers its platform in 10 s each. A discharge places the container after raise, drive in and lower. A load lifts it after drive in and raise.
Every event time of the simulator is compared with the value worked out by hand, and the largest gap must be below a millionth of a second.

cards.title: Four AGVs per crane keep the cranes nearly always busy
cards.lead: The cranes wait less with every AGV added and almost never wait from 12 AGVs on. With 8 AGVs, four per crane, the best rule keeps each crane waiting 5.7 s per container while random dispatching wastes 13.3 s, so the later experiments use 8 AGVs.
cards.body: The yard is long, and each container needs 229 s of AGV work, about 3 crane cycles. Two cranes therefore need at least 6 AGVs even with perfect sharing. With two AGVs per crane the cranes manage 29.4 moves per hour, close to the 30.5 reported by Luo (2016). NV/FCFS stops improving and stays between 12 and 13 s from 8 AGVs on, all of it while load containers are fetched. Its window of three jobs was tuned on the earlier, shorter yard and is tuned again in the next experiment.
details: Two quay cranes each work 2 bays of 25 discharge and then 25 load containers in a fixed order. The planned crane cycle is 75 s. The yard has 50 blocks laid out after Yangshan Phase IV, with the cranes over the middle. Discharge containers go to blocks within 10 of the 5 blocks behind the cranes, and load containers come from blocks within 15. These ranges are an assumption, set so that the cranes reach the productivity reported by Luo (2016). Each AGV takes the nearest free rack of its block, and a rack visit takes 51 s. No randomness.

It is the smallest even fleet at which the good rules leave little waiting while random dispatching still wastes more than twice as much. It also matches Luo (2016), who reports that at least four lift-AGVs per crane are needed for 40 moves per hour. Fleets of 6 and 10 are kept as a scarce and a comfortable case.
The Briskorn inventory rule with phase factor 1.6 (Briskorn et al., 2006), nearest vehicle first come first served (NV/FCFS) with a window of 3 jobs, fixed crane groups, and random dispatching.
30 seeds, with every method run on the same seeds. Means are shown with a 95% confidence interval (t = 2.045).
cards.label: Experiment 2.1 · Fleet size

design.question: How many AGVs do the two cranes need on this yard, and at what fleet size does the choice of dispatcher make a difference?
design.why: Every later experiment runs with one fleet. With too many AGVs, spare vehicles hide every dispatching mistake and all methods look the same. With too few, no method can keep the cranes busy. The comparison is only meaningful in between.
design.vary: The fleet, from 2 to 16 AGVs (1 to 8 per crane), and the dispatching rule, all four rules.
design.fixed: No randomness, so every crane move takes exactly 75 s. Each run has 200 containers on the 50-block yard. Each fleet and rule is run on the same 30 instances.
design.measure: Crane idle time per container, the mean over the 30 instances with its 95% confidence interval.
design.decide: The smallest fleet at which the good rules leave little waiting while random dispatching still wastes clearly more. Checked against the crane productivity reported by Luo (2016).

maths.step: The work an AGV does for one container
maths.text: Each container needs a trip between crane and yard, the drive to the next job, and one rack visit of $r = 51$ s. Here $d$ is the driving time per container, all AGV legs added up and divided by the $n$ containers, averaged over the 30 instances and all fleet sizes.

maths.step: The fewest AGVs that could keep both cranes busy
maths.text: Each crane needs one AGV every $c = 75$ s, and one AGV can serve a container only every $\bar W$ s. So $m = 2$ cranes need at least the number below. It is a lower bound, since it assumes AGVs never wait and are shared perfectly, which is why the cranes still wait with 6 AGVs.

maths.step: From waiting time to crane productivity
maths.text: A crane completes one move every $c$ seconds plus the time $\bar I$ it waits for AGVs, so its moves per hour are given below. With two AGVs per crane this gives about the 30.5 moves per hour reported by *Luo (2016)*.
